summary:
Martinique stands under France's national framework. Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department in full, so identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statutes and the marriage regime operate here as in the metropole. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1815 and the 2013 marriage-equality law applies.

Discrimination protection rests on several instruments that reach the island directly. Goods and services have been covered since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2), employment since Labour Code article L1132-1 in 2008, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, whose wording 'sexual identity' was replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. A National Assembly amendment approved 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comments, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the 1881 Law on the Freedom of the Press to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. The first person convicted under it, MP Christian Vanneste in January 2006, had that conviction cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Nothing in the criminal law criminalises being trans.

Since 1 January 2017 trans people in Martinique can change their legal gender without surgery or a medical diagnosis, but a change of the gender marker still requires an application to a court; a first name change can be handled at the registry office. The enabling bill was signed 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly, with the Constitutional Council ruling it constitutional on 17 November 2016 and striking the original self-certification provision. Before that reform, legal gender change had been prohibited for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France.

Detention is the sharpest visitor-facing risk. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code requires detainees to be held in facilities matching the gender marker on their identity documents, so placement follows the document rather than anatomy, and most trans women are consequently held in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records detainees telling trans women 'we don't want any women here'. The French prison framework governs Martinique's establishments as French law, and this pattern of placement and threat reaches them.

The CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on inspections at which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at four sites, and it makes recommendations on placement, isolation, safety and staff training. Because the opinion addresses French establishments as a category, its findings bind Martinique's prisons too.

Penalties increase where physical assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by imprisonment. A report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims, against about 1,380 in 2018. Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published 1 February 2022.

Gender-affirming healthcare is covered by Sécurité Sociale under ALD 31, but a 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems including extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location. For minors, centre-right Republican senators commissioned a report on youth gender care in March 2024, after which legislation to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024; the Macron government opposed it and no update has appeared since 23 July 2024. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access.

Two national education measures touch trans residents and students. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign against anti-LGBTQ bullying, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day, and in March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms.

Community infrastructure on the island is real but small. JM Concept 972 is a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network providing information, meetings and services, and running private parties and garden parties supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters, with dated events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025. Organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM, alongside the case law, support organisations and country-of-origin experts catalogued on the Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Martinique resource page.
tangentialFactors:
French official hostility toward homosexuality has a documented history that shapes the institutions trans visitors encounter: the 1960 Mirguet amendment treated homosexuality as a 'national scourge' alongside alcoholism, and the Vichy age-of-consent law of 6 August 1942 set 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. Neither provision is in force; both show how quickly codified hostility has been reversed in this framework.

Adjacent national measures adopted since 2021 signal a broad protective turn that does not depend on trans status: assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the MSM blood donation deferral was removed on 16 March 2022. These are LGB-facing provisions and do not alter a trans visitor's entry, document or detention position.

The trajectory of youth gender care is contested in France and is unresolved: a legislative ban passed one chamber in May 2024 and stalled, while specialist society guidelines issued in late 2024 run against the position taken by the Académie Nationale de Médecine. A visitor accompanying or seeking care for a minor should treat this as unsettled rather than settled law.

Local residents use JM Concept 972 for information, meetings and social events, and the overseas-department organisations AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM for support and prevention work. outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records a trans-specific incident inside a Martinique prison. The BuzzFeed News reporting and the CGLPL opinion document French establishments as a category and do not name a facility in Martinique; the CGLPL inspection sites cited in the opinion are on the mainland. The extension of those findings to Martinique rests on the legal point that the French prison framework governs the department's establishments, not on an on-site inspection there.

Whether any French place of deprivation of liberty in Martinique has been inspected for transgender-detainee conditions since the 25 May 2021 opinion is unresolved and not sourced here. The number of transgender detainees held on the island, and any complaints filed by them, are likewise not sourced.

Penalty and offence statistics in the summary (the 36% rise, roughly 1,870 victims in 2019 against about 1,380 in 2018) are national figures for France; no Martinique-specific breakdown of homophobic or transphobic offences is available in the inventory, so the island's own rate is unresolved.

Several items rest on a Wikipedia-sourced account of French law, including the 31 December 2004 hate-speech amendment, the Vanneste conviction and its cancellation, the 1 February 2022 conversion-therapy bill, and the education measures of 2019. These were not checked against the statutes themselves in this pass. The status of the under-18 transition bill is unresolved beyond the last sourced update of 23 July 2024.
